quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

### Verdict on Confidence Calibration

**`confident` is directionally defensible** as the identity tier. The evidence converges strongly on I1:
- Name "Patrick Flynn" — exact match
- Death year 1908 — exact match to I1's established `diedByYear`
- Location Schuylkill County, PA — matches two decades of attested residence (pe_001, pe_004)
- No competing candidate in the tree

**However, the rationale does not adequately support the tier as written.** Three problems were found:

---

### Problems Found

| # | Problem | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Missing mandatory check lines** — The rationale omits the required date check (born ~1845; 0-year gap, consistent, but secondary informant with known birthplace bias) and the residence check (death Schuylkill County vs. attested Schuylkill County — same county). | Required |
| 2 | **Null match_score unexplained** — `same_person` scoring was not recorded, and the rationale offers no explanation. A null score for a reachable persona leaves the entry unverifiable and would flag in a proof-conclusion audit. | Required |
| 3 | **Rationale conflates content with identity evidence** — "Names Thomas Flynn as father" describes what the record says, not why this record belongs to I1. The corroborating census links (pe_001, pe_004) that actually justify `confident` are also absent. | Quality |

---

### Recommended Corrected Rationale

> "Date check: record states born 1845 Pennsylvania (secondary informant — son-in-law, family not present; a_012 bias note flags possible birthplace error, censuses show Ireland); tree person born approx. 1845; gap 0 years, consistent. Residence check: death in Schuylkill County, PA (1908) versus nearest attested residence Schuylkill County, PA (1860 census, pe_004) — same county. Identity: name Patrick Flynn exact match; death year 1908 exact match; location matches multi-decade attested residence. Corroboration: pe_001 (1850 census) and pe_004 (1860 census, Thomas Flynn household) already placed this individual in Schuylkill County; this death certificate closes the life arc. No competing Patrick Flynn of this age and location. Match score: null — same_person scoring step not recorded; must be verified if record is reachable. Informant note: a_013 is secondary hearsay from the son-in-law; this affects the weight of the parentage claim, not the identity of the deceased. `confident` on identity."

---

I now have everything I need. This is review-only mode — I will produce a written analysis only and make no writes.

---

## Review of pe_005 — a_013 → I1 (Patrick Flynn), `confident`

### What pe_005 asserts

pe_005 links assertion a_013 — a `relationship` assertion (fact_type: relationship, value: "Father: Thomas Flynn") extracted from the death certificate for the "deceased" persona — to I1 (Patrick Flynn), at `confident`. The recorded rationale is: *"Death certificate for Patrick Flynn, d. 1908, Schuylkill County. Names match, death location matches known residence. Names Thomas Flynn as father."*

---

### Evidence inventory

**The death certificate record (ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF) has three assertions:**

| Assertion | Fact type | Informant | Quality | Content |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a_011 | Death | Attending physician (witness) | Primary | Died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, PA |
| a_012 | Birth | James Brown, son-in-law (family, not present) | Secondary | Born 1845, Pennsylvania (note: conflicts with census records showing Ireland) |
| a_013 | Relationship | James Brown, son-in-law (family, not present) | Secondary | Father: Thomas Flynn |

**Existing person_evidence for I1:**

- pe_001 (a_001): 1850 census, Schuylkill County — `confident`
- pe_002 (a_004): Same 1850 census, household position — `probable`
- pe_004 (a_010): 1860 census, Thomas Flynn household, Schuylkill County — `confident`
- pe_005 (a_013): This entry under review

**pe_005 match_score:** null (no `same_person` score recorded)

---

### Analysis of the confidence calibration

**The identity question pe_005 addresses:** Is the person listed as "deceased" on this 1908 Schuylkill County death certificate the same individual as I1 (Patrick Flynn)?

The evidence on that identity question is genuinely strong:

- The name Patrick Flynn is an exact match.
- The death year 1908 matches I1's established diedByYear of 1908 exactly.
- The location Schuylkill County, PA matches two decades of prior attested residence from pe_001 and pe_004.
- There is no competing candidate — the tree attests only one Patrick Flynn of this era in this county.

On the identity question alone, `confident` is directionally defensible.

---

### Concerns with pe_005 as written

**1. The two mandatory check lines are absent.** Every pe_ rationale is required to open with a date check and a residence check. Neither appears:

- **Date check:** The record states born 1845, Pennsylvania (secondary informant). The tree person's birth year is approximately 1845. The gap is 0 years — consistent. This should be stated explicitly, including the caveat that the informant is secondary (son-in-law, family not present), and that a_012's bias notes flag a birthplace discrepancy (certificate says Pennsylvania; census records say Ireland — the same informant may have been mistaken on the birth country too).
- **Residence check:** Death in Schuylkill County, PA (1908) versus nearest attested residence (Schuylkill County from the 1850 and 1860 census links). The answer is "same county" — no distance calculation needed. This is straightforward, but the check line should still be written.

**2. The null match_score is unexplained.** The instructions require `same_person` to be called for every reachable persona. pe_005's null is either legitimate (the record was unreachable) or represents an omission of the scoring step. The rationale offers no explanation. An unexplained null leaves a reviewer unable to verify whether the discipline was applied, and the writer tool is documented as now refusing links for reachable personas without a score.

**3. The rationale conflates assertion content with identity evidence.** The line "Names Thomas Flynn as father" is a statement about what the record says, not about why this death certificate belongs to I1. Identity evidence is name, date, place, household position — not the content of what the record reports. This conflation makes the rationale look more complete than it is.

**4. No reference to corroborating prior links.** The pe_001 and pe_004 entries — two decades of census evidence placing Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County — are the strongest reason to be confident this death certificate is about I1. Neither is mentioned. A reviewer reading pe_005 in isolation has no visibility into that corroboration.

**5. Informant quality is not noted.** Confidence measures identity, not informant quality — that distinction is correct. But a_013's informant bias notes flag that this is a son-in-law reporting hearsay about his father-in-law's parentage. That context belongs in the rationale so that downstream work (proof-conclusion, conflict-resolution) can weigh the parentage claim properly.

---

### Verdict on calibration

**`confident` is defensible as the identity tier** for this link — the name, exact death year, location, and corroborating census evidence all converge on I1 as the sole plausible match. The confidence level itself is not obviously wrong.

**However, the rationale does not support the tier as written.** It is missing the mandatory date and residence check lines, offers no explanation for the null match_score, conflates content with identity evidence, and omits the corroborating prior links that actually justify `confident`. If this entry were audited by proof-conclusion, the missing date check and null score would flag it as unverified.

---

### Recommended improved rationale (as text — no write made)

> "Date check: record states born 1845 Pennsylvania (secondary informant — son-in-law, family not present; note a_012 flags that son-in-law may have been mistaken on birthplace, with censuses showing Ireland); tree person born approximately 1845; gap 0 years, consistent. Residence check: death in Schuylkill County, PA (1908) versus nearest attested residence Schuylkill County, PA (1860 census, pe_004) — same county. Identity evidence: name Patrick Flynn exact match; death year 1908 exact match to tree person's established death year; death location Schuylkill County matches multi-decade attested residence. Corroboration: pe_001 (1850 census, Schuylkill County) and pe_004 (1860 census, Thomas Flynn household, Schuylkill County) already established this individual across two censuses in the same county; the death certificate closes the life arc of the same person. No competing Patrick Flynn of this age and location in the tree. Match score: null — same_person scoring step was not recorded; should be verified (if the record is reachable, the score is required). Note on informant: a_013 is secondary information from a son-in-law; the informant quality affects the weight of the parentage claim (Father: Thomas Flynn), not the identity of the deceased. `confident` on the identity question: unique name, exact death year and location match, two corroborating census links."

---

Would you like me to update pe_005's rationale to the text above? The confidence level (`confident`) would stay the same; only the rationale would change. Let me know if you authorise that update, or if you would prefer a different formulation.

---

The 1908 death certificate has been matched to Patrick Flynn at the "very likely the same person" level — the name, death year, and county all line up precisely, and two earlier census records from the same county already identified him through 1850 and 1860. The match itself is sound, but the written explanation recorded for it is thin and is missing some required checks that prove the reasoning was done; it should be revised before the case is closed.
